name: Jewish Neo-Aramaic dialect of Urmi, 'J. Urmi'

catalog_quote: 1.11.1. Nouns, Pronouns, Adjectives and Numerals. In most multisyllabic nouns, pronouns, adjectives and numerals the stress is placed on either the final or the penultimate syllable. Word-final stress position, which is found in words in all contexts, may be regarded as the basic one. It is the usual position in words of these categories that occur in pause before an intonation group boundary and also in the citation form of nominals. The retraction of stress to an earlier syllable is typically found in words in non-pausal position in the middle of an intonation group or at least within the middle of a syntactic or discourse unit. ... The normal position for the stress in annexation forms of nouns is on the penultimate syllable ... 1.11.3. Verbs. (i) The basic position of the stress in verb forms derived from the present base (§4.2.3.) is on the syllable with the vowel nucleus that occurs before the final radical of the root or, if the vowel of this syllable is elided when an inflectional suffix is added, on the first syllable of the suffix ... (iv) Compound verbal forms, which have a resultative participle or an infinitive as their base, have a different pattern of stress. It is placed on the syllable with the vowel nucleus that occurs after the final radical of the root, which is a pattern that is characteristic of nominals ... When further pronominal suffixes are added to the verbal forms just described, the basic position of stress remains the same
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nominals (nouns, pronouns, adjectives, numerals) and adverbials: basic stress is word-final (citation form, pausal position), retracting to the penult in non-pausal position inside an intonation group. Verbs: stress sits on the root vowel before the last radical (which is the final syllable in suffixless forms such as +qatə́l 'he kills', imperative +qtúl 'kill!'), moving to the first suffix syllable only when that vowel is elided (+qatlá 'she kills'); further pronominal/TAM suffixes leave it in place (+qatə́llu 'he kills them'). Khan's own summaries (2008 Introduction; 2018 p.19) call this 'general placement of the stress in word final position', a defining trans-Zab Jewish feature attributed to Kurdish/Turkic contact.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress in the accessible snippets; Khan distinguishes nuclear vs non-nuclear (intonation-group) stress and describes stress groups (numeral + noun, negator + verb) in sec. 1.12.
new_statements.exceptions: Retraction of nominal stress to the penultimate outside pause / mid intonation group (e.g. onto the indefinite marker); verbs keep stress on the root syllable when suffixes are added, so suffixed verb forms are not word-final; stress is morphologically contrastive (Jastrow 1997: J. Azerbaijan zdélu 'they feared' vs zdelú 'their fear'). Snippet vowel diacritics in the verb examples are scanned-rendered ('+qatál' in the raw snippet = Khan's +qatə́l).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress as marked in Khan's text transcriptions; word-final is explicitly the citation-form and pre-pausal position for nominals, with discourse-conditioned retraction inside intonation groups. The sibling catalog entry for Jewish Sanandaj (hula1244), built on Khan's near-identically worded 2009 description, was coded set by morphology; either label is defensible here, fixed: final syllable chosen because the describer himself names word-final as the basic/default position.
new_statements.identity_note: Khan 2008 describes specifically the Jewish dialect of the town of Urmi (NW Iran; speakers recorded in Israel) = NENA database dialect 79 'Urmi, Jewish'; Garbell 1965 and Jastrow 1997 ('Jewish Azerbaijan') cover the wider Jewish Persian-Azerbaijan group (Urmi, Salmas, Bashkale; southern Solduz/Naghada, Šino/Oshnaviyeh, Sablagh/Mahabad). All fall under Glottolog lish1246 Lishán Didán / ISO trg (Northern trans-Zab Jewish NENA). Not to be confused with Christian Urmi (Assyrian Neo-Aramaic, penultimate stress) described in Khan 2016.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (Khan 2008 sec. 1.11: word-final stress basic in nominals, retraction conditioned by morphology/syntax; catalog classification morphological) and with the statement held by the project ('fixed: final syllable'): Garbell 1965 likewise gives ultimate stress as the general/default position and states that placement is morphologically conditioned, adding explicit non-final classes (-ušum nouns penultimate; unstressed verbal suffix -wa). No contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Garbell: stress placement is morphologically conditioned; the default (unmarked) position is the final syllable -- simplex forms, verb forms with zero suffix and prefixed forms are stressed on the ultima, and she marks stress only where it is NOT final; listed non-final classes include penultimate stress in nouns in -ušum (awrúšum, qurqúšum) and verb forms where a suffix such as past -wa is unstressed (zíl-wa 'he had gone', pérwa, dárwa). Phrase/word-group ('syntactic') stress and pitch are deferred to ch. 4 Syntactophonology (not visible).
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing visible in the snippets; stress is said to be accompanied by raised pitch
new_statements.exceptions: penultimate stress (a) in nouns ending in -ušum (awrúšum 'silk', qurqúšum 'lead'), (b) further classes cut off by the snippet; verbal forms with the suffix -wa keep stress on the stem (zíl-wa, pérwa, dárwa); 'It is conditioned morphologically'
new_statements.identity_note: Garbell 1965 describes the Jewish North-Eastern Neo-Aramaic of (northern) Persian Azerbaijan -- Urmi and neighbouring towns (the Lishan Didan / J. Urmi cluster, Glottolog lish1246), from speakers resettled in Israel; the catalog record (Khan 2008) is specifically the Urmi town dialect of the same cluster.

sources.quote: Unlike all other known NENA dialects, including the most archaizing among them, e.g. Qaraqosh, Alqosh and Tyare, where word stress is generally penultimate in nominal forms, Trans-Zab exhibits a shift of word stress from the penultimate to the ultimate syllable in the nominal system (with some exceptions, chiefly adverbs), most probably due to the influence of Kurdish and (in J.Az.) also of Azerbaijani.
